newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds firmer in line with Europe.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds firmer in line with Europe.

text.p: Irish bonds firmed up slightly in moderate buying trade on Tuesday in line with bonds across Europe, which opened weaker but recouped their losses and pushed higher later in the session, dealers said.
"European bonds seem to be resisting the decline of U.S. bonds and the Irish market has followed that," a dealer said. "Otherwise, there's not much fresh news or data about to give direction."
Bond markets had largely shrugged off Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's comments yesterday about liquidating U.S. bonds, the dealer said.
Later insistence by Hashimoto that his comments had been misinterpreted helped gilts and U.S. Treasuries.
By 1500 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 10 pence at 102.09 to yield 5.92 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up three pence at 109.90 to yield 6.52 percent.
Yields against German Bunds were unchanged from Monday's close at 156 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 90 over in the 10-year.

Dealers said the Irish market was beginning to look towards next week's exchequer returns which are likely to show a large budget surplus at mid-year and highlight that there will be limited issuance of fresh stock over the balance of the year.
Attention would be focussed this week on the new Irish government, set to take office on Thursday - specifically on the incoming finance minister, dealers said.

"The market wants to see who the minister will be and what he or she is going to do about the currency, which has been causing Irish bonds to underperform Spain and Italy over the past six weeks or so."
It looked increasingly as though European currencies would be locked into EMU at central parity, the dealer said, which would necessitate an upward adjustment of the Irish pound.
Dealers expect a quiet couple of weeks for the market as the new government settles in.
